title: Sablière: a new 0% alcohol sparkling ‘wine’ designed from first principles
summary: Website: https://sabliere.co.uk/ I’ve written quite a bit about the attempts to make interesting, complex dealcoholized wines. There’s another approach, which
content:
Website: https://sabliere.co.uk/

I’ve written quite a bit about the attempts to make interesting, complex dealcoholized wines. There’s another approach, which is purpose-built proxies: complex non-wine drinks that operate in the same space as wine.

And this week I met up with Lucy Isles, co-owner of a new brand, Sablière, which is built from the ground up after a lot of research to behave just like a good Champagne or sparkling wine.

Lucy emphasizes that this is not a sparkling tea or a kombucha, but something that has been put together after a lengthy research journey.

Her partner in this venture is Kim Wilson, who studied brewing technology at Heriot Watt University, and then worked for Diageo. Sablière is made in their own facility in Edinburgh.

The challenge they faced is one that’s common to anyone working in the zero alcohol space. Without alcohol, they have no viscosity, no sterility, no mouthfeel and no texture.

She describes the research journey as a ‘wonderful multidisciplinary experience’.

They have worked with innovative South African winemaker Bruce Jack, with a microbiologist from Lallemand in Denmark, an Edinburgh University physicist looking at bubbles, and Andrew Gardner, a tea specialist (a tea specialist).

‘We were really trying to think, how can we do something novel here?’ says Lucy.

So, their first pair of sparkling wines are now live. These are meant to be wine replacements, and they are beginning to look at how they can also do this with still white and red wines.

The wines are built up using four key ingredients. There’s tea, which gives length. There are apples, for body. Honey gives aroma. And, finally, verjus gives acidity. They finish by carbonating to 6 bars pressure, the same as Champagne.

There are two expressions so far. One is a Blanc de Blancs style, which they based on Ruinart, and the other is a rosé based on Charles Heidsieck.

The Blanc is a blend of white teas, and they worked with tea sommelier Joyce Maina to select these. There are white curls from Nepal, and white peony from China. They extract the teas in house, using a different process for each. The verjus is from Sussex, which adds viscosity and acidity, and this is balanced with malic acid from cox apples. They use a range of yeasts from Lallemand to give some wine-like qualities, but this fermentation produces no alcohol.

One key decision was to go for 0.0% alcohol rather than 0.5% because of the Middle East market.

The final element is blossom honey distillate, adding sweetness but not sugary weight. Altogether the Blanc and Rosé have 37 g/l sugar. So they are sterile filtered. There are no added sulfites, but some sulfites are used by the verjus producer: they are looking to see whether they could eliminate these sulfites too.

What does it taste like? It has lovely aromas: fruity, herby and aromatic with some honeyed notes, floral elements and a touch of green. The palate is fresh and textured and you get the honey and tea notes, but also nice fruitiness and good acidity. Very stylish and fruit driven.

The rosé has Kentish kiss apples which give some pink notes. Four teas are used: mountain oolong (smoky, oxidized notes), gold curl, wild lapsang and da hong pao (delicate caramel).

It’s a golden colour with a slight pink hue. There’s a fruity, herby note on the nose with red apple, mandarin and dried herbs. In the mouth there’s nice bite with some structure and good acidity, and nice herby complexity. There’s even a slight caramel twist. This is really good.

I wouldn’t mistake either for Champagne, but these are high quality, intentional sparkling ‘wines’ that are quite friendly and offer a bit of complexity. Sablière are selling direct to customers at £32 for the Blanc and £35 for the Rosé. They launched quietly in January, their website was launched in April, and they already have 20 clients (restaurants and retail).

title: Highlights: the chillable Olivier Coste Bisou Rouge 2025
summary: This is great: a delicious, drinkable Languedoc red designed to be drunk chilled. Olivier Coste Bisou Rouge 2025 Pays d’Oc,
content:
This is great: a delicious, drinkable Languedoc red designed to be drunk chilled.

Olivier Coste Bisou Rouge 2025 Pays d’Oc, France
11.5% alcohol. This is designed to be served chilled, and the lips on the front label change from red to blue when it’s at the right temperature. It’s a lighter-style red with low tannins, but it’s still a red wine. Lovely floral, sappy, sweet cherry and berry fruits, and nice weight on the palate. Crunchy and delicious; fruity and enjoyable. There’s a touch of sweetness and it is juicy and easy, but satisfying. Really impressive. 91/100

title: The wines of Zacharioudakis, Crete
summary: Website: https://www.zacharioudakis.com/en/ Zacharioudakis is a family-owned winery from northern Crete, near Heraklion. It was started in 2000 by journalist Stelios
content:
Website: https://www.zacharioudakis.com/en/

Zacharioudakis is a family-owned winery from northern Crete, near Heraklion. It was started in 2000 by journalist Stelios Zacharioudakis, and since 2009 it has been his full time job. The 20 hectares of organically farmed vineyards are at an altitude of 500 metres, which tempers the hot climate.

Zacharioudakis Codex White 2024 Crete, Greece
In a striking white bottle. This is 80% Assyrtiko, 20% Muscat Spinas. Lively and bright with crisp citrus fruit. Tart, with some grapey detail. Nice purity here. 89/100

Zacharioudakis Assyrtiko 2023 Crete, Greece
13% alcohol. Dense with fresh lemony fruit and some pithiness. Has a bit of grip. 89/100

Zacharioudakis Orthi Petra 2024 Crete, Greece
A blend of Sauvignon Blanc and Vidiano. Crisp and bright with lemony fruit. Tart, showing nice intensity and some herby hints. 88/100

Zacharioudakis Vidiano 2023 Crete, Greece
5 months in French oak. Juicy, lively and bright with nice focus and a hint of mint, some herbs, and a nice acid line. Has a bit of structure. 90/100

Zacharioudakis Victoria Rosé 2024 Crete, Greece
70% Cabernet Sauvignon, 30% Kotsifali. Juicy and bright with some tartness. Bright red cherry and plum fruit with good focus and acidity. 88/100

Zacharioudakis Codex Red 2022 Crete, Greece
14% alcohol. In a black bottle. Syrah, Merlot and Kotsifali. Juicy, bright and fresh with a chalky mineral edge to the fruit. Nice purity. 90/100

Zacharioudakis Kotsifali 2021 Crete, Greece
14% alcohol. 8 months in oak. Lighter in colour, this is juicy and bright with good acidity. It’s fruity and expressive with a nice savoury twist. 92/100

title: Reynolds Wine Growers: top wines from the cooler north of Portugal’s Alentejo
summary: Website: https://reynoldswinegrowers.com/en/ Reynolds Wine Growers is a significant producer, with a 200 hectare farm in Figuera de Cima, with 40
content:
Website: https://reynoldswinegrowers.com/en/

Reynolds Wine Growers is a significant producer, with a 200 hectare farm in Figuera de Cima, with 40 hectares of vines. One of the benefits of the location is altitude, at 600 m. This is next to Serra de São Mamede Natural Park, Portalegre, in the north of the region. They also have two other smaller vineyards in other locations.

It’s currently being run by Julian Reynolds, whose grandfather, Thomas Reynolds, introduced Alicante Bouschet into Portugal. This is the same Reynolds family that was behind another Alentejo winery, Mouchão. I tasted these wines with Julian.

Yields are low at 3.5 tons/ha. They pick by variety, and don’t crush any of the grapes, just destem. Whites are fermented and aged in stainless steel, while reds are fermented in large oak, then do malolactic in barrel.

Reynolds Wine Growers Gloria Reynolds Art & Tradition Branco 2021 Alentejo, Portugal
This is Antão Vaz. Nice intensity on the nose, with pear and peach fruit. There’s lovely fruity depth on the palate with a spicy, savoury edge. Grainy and chiselled with a lovely fruit core. 94/100

Reynolds Wine Growers Alicante Bouschet Grande Reserva ‘Julian Reynolds’ 2016 Alentejo, Portugal
There’s a bit of Syrah in the mix here. Beautiful floral intensity on the nose, which is fine and sweetly aromatic. The palate has freshness and density with real elegance. Such purity, this is ageing really well, and has a long way still to go. 96/100

Reynolds Wine Growers Alicante Bouschet Grande Reserva ‘Julian Reynolds’ 2005 Alentejo, Portugal
Nice development on the nose with some iodine and spice. Quite mineral with sweet berry fruits. Has tannins still, and savoury notes of spice, earth and iodine. Fresh, mineral and complex with great intensity. Fully developed, but still alive. 95/100

Reynolds Wine Growers Gloria Reynolds Art & Tradition 2014 Alentejo, Portugal
100% Alicante, two years in Seguin Moreau Icône Elégance barrels. Concentrated and fresh, and still taut and focused, with blackcurrant and black cherry fruit with good density and tannins. Focused, with a firm, grippy finish. So lovely and full of interest. 95/100

Reynolds Wine Growers Gloria Reynolds Cathedral 2005 Alentejo, Portugal
They release 2000 bottles of this and keep the rest for friends and family. Alicante Bouschet. Still deeply coloured with a slight savoury edge to the nose. Earth, malt and soy sauce notes on the nose as well as vivid fruit. The palate is concentrated and dense with some nice grip. Bold and vivid with a savoury twist, and fully mature. 93/100

title: Highlights: Château Marquis de Terme Margaux 2022
summary: I don’t buy a lot of Bordeaux, but when I find a good one, I find it really satisfying. This
content:
I don’t buy a lot of Bordeaux, but when I find a good one, I find it really satisfying. This one was on the shelf at a Leclerc in Lourdes, France, and I thought it would be worth the €48 it was listed at. It was.

Château Marquis de Terme Margaux 2022 Bordeaux, France
13% alcohol. This is quite lovely. Really primary with juicy blackcurrant and redcurrant fruit, with a touch of spicy oak as well as some nice acidity. Good concentration and focus here, with good tannins. Focused, fresh and so youthful, and I think this will age beautifully over the next decade, and perhaps longer. It’s not a big, rich wine (13%!), but it’s serious, and the sort of wine critics miss at primeurs. 93/100

title: Exploring Beaumes-de-Venise (1) introducing this interesting Rhône Cru
summary: Beaumes-de-Venise is a small but interesting Cru in the southern Rhône. Initially, it was made a cru for its sweet
content:
Beaumes-de-Venise is a small but interesting Cru in the southern Rhône.

Initially, it was made a cru for its sweet wines, vins doux naturels based on Muscat, back in 1945. The Cru emerged that year, but wines from 1943 onwards were allowed to use it. Still, to this day, the Muscats from here are highly prized.

Then, as recently as 2005, it became a Cru for red wines too.

Since 2022 they have had the paperwork in for dry white wines to also have the cru, and there’s a lot of interest in this. It’s going to happen soon! The rules for the whites will be that there must be a minimum of 5% Muscat, and a maximum of 30%.

This is a diverse cru, with vineyards ranging from 50 m in the south (prime Muscat territory) where it’s a bit flatter, all the way up to 600 m. Aspects and soils change frequently, as the northern part of the cru is quite hilly.

Soils vary, with some quite sandy, others clay rich, some with a bit of limestone, and then there’s a famous soil type that’s much prized called trias (you might even see this on labels). It’s specific to this cru in the Rhône, and it’s a blond/yellow sort of ferricrete that can be quite hard. It needs to be worked after rain.

I began with a tour with winegrower Xavier Vignon on an all-terrain vehicle, and over a period of three hours we investigated just about every bit of the cru, from the low-lying Muscat vineyards of the south to the high-up bits tucked into the dentelles.

BEAUMES-DE-VENISE

  • Introduction
  • Petitjean family: Domaine de Cassan and Château Les Croix des Pins
  • Xavier Vignon
  • Domaine La Ligière
  • Domaine Saint Amant
  • Domaine de la Ferme Saint-Martin
  • Domaine Raboly

Gilvesy Váradi Furmint NV Szent György-Hegy, Hungary
11.5% alcohol. This is quite beautiful: linear with a distinct stony minerality, crystalline lemon fruit and real precision. title: Biofiltro: cleaning up winery waste water with worm power, creating high-quality compost at the same time
summary: Website: https://biofiltro.be/ Biofiltro is an innovative way of dealing with winery waste water. And the bonus is that because it
content:
Website: https://biofiltro.be/

Biofiltro is an innovative way of dealing with winery waste water. And the bonus is that because it is worm-based, it creates vermicast, a high quality organic fertilizer at the same time.

I caught up with Arnaud Maurissen at Domaine Lafage in the Roussillon to see how it works. Lafage have been pioneers in implementing this system in France. Previously, I’d seen it in action in Chile at Montes.

They now have 100 installations in vineyards and other places. They began in the USA and Chile, and have now started in Europe.

The winery waste water first goes to a lagoon, and the pH is adjusted to make it worm compatible. pH 7 is ideal; normally the winery water is pH 5.5-7.5. Then this water goes to a large basin that’s full of woodchips. The woodchips can’t be too small because they need air flow in the system, and want to avoid them being compacted.

The worms are initially inoculated at 500 g per square meter. They then begin digesting the wood chips, and in turn produce vermicast, a high quality compost. The waste water is fed over the chips in a steady flow. The worms remove the organic compounds from this waste water and this biological filtration makes it fit for use in irrigation.

From time to time they harvest the vermicast. The worms mostly live in the top 20cm, so they remove this and put it aside. They then collect the vermicast (the system produces 500 kg per square meter, and the basin is 400 m2). They then put in new woodchips and add the worms and woodchips back.

This system consumes much less energy than the regular winery wastewater treatment. It also produces the vermicast and also water for irrigation (10 000 m3 per year).

For an up-to-date review of the science of winery waste water treatment, this is a useful article: https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4441/18/4/504

title: Highlights: Soalheiro Ag.hora Alvarinho 2022 Vinho Verde, Portugal
summary: Soalheiro Ag.hora Alvarinho 2022 Vinho Verde, Portugal11.5% alcohol. A collaboration with Gio Chezade, from Georgia but now resident in Portugal.
content:
Soalheiro Ag.hora Alvarinho 2022 Vinho Verde, Portugal
11.5% alcohol. A collaboration with Gio Chezade, from Georgia but now resident in Portugal. This wine spends 2 months on skins in amphora with some stems, and then ages 9 months in the same vessel. It has some stony minerality and a touch of green apple as well as some citrus and pear fruit. Nice tension here with some subtle oxidative notes and then some salinity on the finish. Beautiful presence. 93/100

title: Revisiting the wines of Doran Vineyards, Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
summary: Website: https://www.doranvineyards.com/home/ Back in 2010 Edwin Doran bought a vineyard in Voor Paardeberg as a retirement gift to himself. Sadly,
content:
Website: https://www.doranvineyards.com/home/

Back in 2010 Edwin Doran bought a vineyard in Voor Paardeberg as a retirement gift to himself. Sadly, he passed last year, but his son Tom has taken on the project. The new GM, Ernie Manuel, was previously in charge of the organic conversion at Mullineux, after a spell working with Joostenberg. So they are working in a more regenerative direction in the vineyards, and these wines are a step up from the 2024s that I tried last year, with the exception of the Chenin Reserve, but this could have been a bottle issue.

Doran Vineyards Ayra 2025 Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
13% alcohol. Chenin Blanc raised in stainless steel. Highly aromatic with primary pear drop notes and some citrus. Textured, full palate with sweet pear and citrus fruit as well as some yellow plum. Nice purity and presence with a rounded mid-palate. 89/100

Doran Vineyards Chenin Reserve 2025 Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
13% alcohol. Wild ferment and ageing in Serbian oak. Some apple, herb and spice on the nose, with a touch of wood. Some juiciness on the palate showing ripe yellow fruits, but the savoury woody notes stick out a little bit, and there are some appley oxidative notes, too. 85/100

Doran Vineyards Rosie D 2025 Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
10% alcohol. This is Grenache Noir raised in stainless steel. Pale pink in colour, this is bright, fresh and fruity with some juiciness and a touch of red cherry alongside the pear and citrus fruit. Light and direct, and I like the fact that the alcohol has been dialled back a bit. 88/100

Doran Vineyards Romy D 2024 Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
13.5% alcohol. Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah raised in old oak. There’s an attractive green sappy edge to the nose. The palate is bright, easy and juicy with attractive red cherry and berry fruits and a touch of blackcurrant, with nice sweetness. Easy and approachable with a bit of crunch on the finish. 90/100

Doran Vineyards Pinotage 2024 Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
13.5% alcohol. Wild yeast ferment, matured in used oak. Supple, ripe cherries and berries with nice texture on the mid-palate. Very appealing with a core of sweet strawberry and cherry fruit, and nice soft tannins. Lots to like about this friendly, approachable red. 90/100

Doran Vineyards Iosa 2024 Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
14% alcohol. A blend of Shiraz and Merlot aged in older oak barrels. Lovely sweet cherries and berries with some floral aromatics. There’s a leafy green edge here with nice berry fruits and then a bit of spice on the finish. A real crowd-pleaser with nice sweet, pure fruit. 91/100

Since 2022 they have had the paperwork in for dry white wines to also have the cru, and there’s a lot of interest in this. It’s going to happen soon! The rules for the whites will be that there must be a minimum of 5% Muscat, and a maximum of 30%.

This is a diverse cru, with vineyards ranging from 50 m in the south (prime Muscat territory) where it’s a bit flatter, all the way up to 600 m. Aspects and soils change frequently, as the northern part of the cru is quite hilly.

Soils vary, with some quite sandy, others clay rich, some with a bit of limestone, and then there’s a famous soil type that’s much prized called trias (you might even see this on labels). It’s specific to this cru in the Rhône, and it’s a blond/yellow sort of ferricrete that can be quite hard. It needs to be worked after rain.

I began with a tour with winegrower Xavier Vignon on an all-terrain vehicle, and over a period of three hours we investigated just about every bit of the cru, from the low-lying Muscat vineyards of the south to the high-up bits tucked into the dentelles.

title: Biofiltro: cleaning up winery waste water with worm power, creating high-quality compost at the same time
summary: Website: https://biofiltro.be/ Biofiltro is an innovative way of dealing with winery waste water. And the bonus is that because it
content:
Website: https://biofiltro.be/

Biofiltro is an innovative way of dealing with winery waste water. And the bonus is that because it is worm-based, it creates vermicast, a high quality organic fertilizer at the same time.

I caught up with Arnaud Maurissen at Domaine Lafage in the Roussillon to see how it works. Lafage have been pioneers in implementing this system in France. Previously, I’d seen it in action in Chile at Montes.

They now have 100 installations in vineyards and other places. They began in the USA and Chile, and have now started in Europe.

The winery waste water first goes to a lagoon, and the pH is adjusted to make it worm compatible. pH 7 is ideal; normally the winery water is pH 5.5-7.5. Then this water goes to a large basin that’s full of woodchips. The woodchips can’t be too small because they need air flow in the system, and want to avoid them being compacted.

The worms are initially inoculated at 500 g per square meter. They then begin digesting the wood chips, and in turn produce vermicast, a high quality compost. The waste water is fed over the chips in a steady flow. The worms remove the organic compounds from this waste water and this biological filtration makes it fit for use in irrigation.

From time to time they harvest the vermicast. The worms mostly live in the top 20cm, so they remove this and put it aside. They then collect the vermicast (the system produces 500 kg per square meter, and the basin is 400 m2). They then put in new woodchips and add the worms and woodchips back.

This system consumes much less energy than the regular winery wastewater treatment. It also produces the vermicast and also water for irrigation (10 000 m3 per year).

For an up-to-date review of the science of winery waste water treatment, this is a useful article: https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4441/18/4/504

title: Highlights: Soalheiro Ag.hora Alvarinho 2022 Vinho Verde, Portugal
summary: Soalheiro Ag.hora Alvarinho 2022 Vinho Verde, Portugal11.5% alcohol. A collaboration with Gio Chezade, from Georgia but now resident in Portugal.
content:
Soalheiro Ag.hora Alvarinho 2022 Vinho Verde, Portugal
11.5% alcohol. A collaboration with Gio Chezade, from Georgia but now resident in Portugal. This wine spends 2 months on skins in amphora with some stems, and then ages 9 months in the same vessel. It has some stony minerality and a touch of green apple as well as some citrus and pear fruit. Nice tension here with some subtle oxidative notes and then some salinity on the finish. Beautiful presence. 93/100

title: Revisiting the wines of Doran Vineyards, Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
summary: Website: https://www.doranvineyards.com/home/ Back in 2010 Edwin Doran bought a vineyard in Voor Paardeberg as a retirement gift to himself. Sadly,
content:
Website: https://www.doranvineyards.com/home/

Back in 2010 Edwin Doran bought a vineyard in Voor Paardeberg as a retirement gift to himself. Sadly, he passed last year, but his son Tom has taken on the project. The new GM, Ernie Manuel, was previously in charge of the organic conversion at Mullineux, after a spell working with Joostenberg. So they are working in a more regenerative direction in the vineyards, and these wines are a step up from the 2024s that I tried last year, with the exception of the Chenin Reserve, but this could have been a bottle issue.

Doran Vineyards Ayra 2025 Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
13% alcohol. Chenin Blanc raised in stainless steel. Highly aromatic with primary pear drop notes and some citrus. Textured, full palate with sweet pear and citrus fruit as well as some yellow plum. Nice purity and presence with a rounded mid-palate. 89/100

Doran Vineyards Chenin Reserve 2025 Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
13% alcohol. Wild ferment and ageing in Serbian oak. Some apple, herb and spice on the nose, with a touch of wood. Some juiciness on the palate showing ripe yellow fruits, but the savoury woody notes stick out a little bit, and there are some appley oxidative notes, too. 85/100

Doran Vineyards Rosie D 2025 Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
10% alcohol. This is Grenache Noir raised in stainless steel. Pale pink in colour, this is bright, fresh and fruity with some juiciness and a touch of red cherry alongside the pear and citrus fruit. Light and direct, and I like the fact that the alcohol has been dialled back a bit. 88/100

Doran Vineyards Romy D 2024 Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
13.5% alcohol. Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah raised in old oak. There’s an attractive green sappy edge to the nose. The palate is bright, easy and juicy with attractive red cherry and berry fruits and a touch of blackcurrant, with nice sweetness. Easy and approachable with a bit of crunch on the finish. 90/100

Doran Vineyards Pinotage 2024 Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
13.5% alcohol. Wild yeast ferment, matured in used oak. Supple, ripe cherries and berries with nice texture on the mid-palate. Very appealing with a core of sweet strawberry and cherry fruit, and nice soft tannins. Lots to like about this friendly, approachable red. 90/100

Doran Vineyards Iosa 2024 Voor Paardeberg, South Africa
14% alcohol. A blend of Shiraz and Merlot aged in older oak barrels. Lovely sweet cherries and berries with some floral aromatics. There’s a leafy green edge here with nice berry fruits and then a bit of spice on the finish. A real crowd-pleaser with nice sweet, pure fruit. 91/100
